passage: Three weeks after Saurabh's father died, his classmates were talking about the fest again, and nobody asked how he was. It hurt. In the canteen he told two friends, "I'm not okay. I don't need advice. Just sit with me sometimes." They did. At home his mother handed him the bank papers and the electricity bill as if he were the grown-up. Saurabh felt proud and heavy at once, and told her he would help but wanted his uncles involved so that he was not doing everything alone. At night he asked the ceiling, "How could God let him go?" and felt a little ashamed of his anger. He told an elder relative, who said the questions were allowed and that they could sit with them together. In the library Gurleen, who had lost her friend Sachin last term, showed him a letter in her notebook. She kept replaying the last chat, when she had left his message unanswered. She wrote the letter to Sachin, read it out to Saurabh, and told him about the day they had laughed on the terrace. Saurabh listened, then shared a memory of his father laughing at his own bad jokes.

qa.q: What did Saurabh ask his two friends to do?
qa.a: He asked them to just sit with him sometimes.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's needs with his classmates differ from what his mother needed from him?
qa.a: With classmates who had moved on, he named what he needed and asked them to sit with him; with his mother, who leaned on him as if he were the grown-up, he offered help but brought in his uncles so that he would not carry it alone.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she kept replaying the last chat with Sachin?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sad, regretting that she had left his message unanswered.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do next to carry her guilt?
qa.a: She could keep sharing memories of Sachin, talk with people she trusts like Saurabh and remind herself that she could not have known.

grounding: Two grieving students show peers' indifference, a parent's leaning, anger at God and guilt over a last message to a friend who died.
